docs.title: Secure ArgoCD JWT Tokens for Cursor MCP
docs.text: When using the ArgoCD MCP server in Cursor, the default configuration stores the API token as plaintext in ~/.cursor/mcp.json. This guide covers multiple approaches to secure the token properly.

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
A typical mcp.json config exposes the token in plain sight:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "argocd-mcp": {
      "command": "/opt/homebrew/bin/npx",
      "args": ["argocd-mcp@latest", "stdio"],
      "env": {
        "ARGOCD_BASE_URL": "https://localhost:8080",
        "ARGOCD_API_TOKEN": "eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIs..."
      }
    }
  }
}

Anyone with read access to this file — or any process that scans config directories — can extract the token and gain full ArgoCD admin access.

docs.title: How ArgoCD MCP Authentication Works
docs.text:
The ArgoCD MCP server is a Node.js process that Cursor spawns and communicates with over stdin/stdout (JSON-RPC). It reads ARGOCD_API_TOKEN from its environment, then uses it as a Bearer token against the ArgoCD REST API.

The token itself is a JWT (JSON Web Token) — a base64url-encoded JSON payload signed with ArgoCD's server secret:

header.payload.signature

A decoded payload looks like:

{
  "iss": "argocd",
  "sub": "admin:apiKey",
  "iat": 1780562370,
  "jti": "01ded6ae-ad7f-4d76-b7e7-d1c8430aca9b"
}

The key insight: the MCP server only needs the token as an environment variable at startup. This means we can inject it dynamically rather than storing it in a file.

docs.title: Solution 1 — macOS Keychain (Recommended)
docs.text: The most secure approach for local development on macOS. The token is encrypted at rest and protected by your login password or Touch ID.

docs.title: Store the token
docs.text:
security add-generic-password \
  -a "argocd-mcp" \
  -s "argocd-api-token" \
  -w "eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIs..." \
  -T ""

docs.title: Create a wrapper script
docs.text:
mkdir -p ~/.local/bin
cat > ~/.local/bin/argocd-mcp-start.sh << 'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
export ARGOCD_BASE_URL="https://localhost:8080"
export ARGOCD_API_TOKEN=$(security find-generic-password -a "argocd-mcp" -s "argocd-api-token" -w)
export NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED=0
exec /opt/homebrew/bin/npx argocd-mcp@latest stdio
EOF
chmod 700 ~/.local/bin/argocd-mcp-start.sh

docs.title: Update mcp.json
docs.text:
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "argocd-mcp": {
      "command": "/Users/<you>/.local/bin/argocd-mcp-start.sh",
      "args": [],
      "env": {
        "PATH": "/opt/homebrew/bin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin"
      }
    }
  }
}

Why this works with Cursor

GUI apps on macOS don't inherit shell environment variables. A wrapper script sidesteps this by resolving the token at process spawn time — before the MCP server starts reading stdin.

docs.title: Rotate the token
docs.text:
# Generate a new token
argocd account generate-token --account admin > /dev/null

# Update the keychain entry
security delete-generic-password -a "argocd-mcp" -s "argocd-api-token"
security add-generic-password -a "argocd-mcp" -s "argocd-api-token" -w "$(argocd account generate-token --account admin)"

docs.title: Solution 2 — .env File with Restricted Permissions
docs.text: Simpler but less secure than the keychain approach. Suitable when keychain access is impractical.

docs.title: Create a secured env file
docs.text:
mkdir -p ~/.config/argocd-mcp
cat > ~/.config/argocd-mcp/.env << 'EOF'
ARGOCD_API_TOKEN=eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIs...
EOF
chmod 600 ~/.config/argocd-mcp/.env

docs.title: Create the wrapper script
docs.text:
cat > ~/.local/bin/argocd-mcp-start.sh << 'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
set -a
source ~/.config/argocd-mcp/.env
set +a
export ARGOCD_BASE_URL="https://localhost:8080"
export NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED=0
exec /opt/homebrew/bin/npx argocd-mcp@latest stdio
EOF
chmod 700 ~/.local/bin/argocd-mcp-start.sh

Warning

Add ~/.config/argocd-mcp/.env to your global gitignore (~/.gitignore_global) to prevent accidental commits.

docs.title: Solution 3 — 1Password / Bitwarden CLI
docs.text:
If you already use a password manager with CLI support:

1PasswordBitwarden 
#!/bin/bash
export ARGOCD_BASE_URL="https://localhost:8080"
export ARGOCD_API_TOKEN=$(op read "op://DevVault/ArgoCD MCP/token")
export NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED=0
exec /opt/homebrew/bin/npx argocd-mcp@latest stdio

#!/bin/bash
export ARGOCD_BASE_URL="https://localhost:8080"
export ARGOCD_API_TOKEN=$(bw get password "argocd-api-token")
export NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED=0
exec /opt/homebrew/bin/npx argocd-mcp@latest stdio

Note

Both CLIs may prompt for biometric or master password unlock on first access per session.

docs.title: Solution 4 — Short-Lived Tokens (Most Secure)
docs.text:
Generate a token that auto-expires each time the MCP server starts:

#!/bin/bash
export ARGOCD_BASE_URL="https://localhost:8080"
export NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED=0

# Generate a token valid for 24 hours
export ARGOCD_API_TOKEN=$(argocd account generate-token \
  --account admin \
  --expires-in 24h \
  --server localhost:8080 \
  --insecure 2>/dev/null)

exec /opt/homebrew/bin/npx argocd-mcp@latest stdio

Tip

This requires the argocd CLI to have a valid session (via argocd login). The generated token expires automatically — even if leaked, the blast radius is limited.

docs.title: Comparison
docs.text: Approach Security Complexity GUI Launch Token Rotation macOS Keychain High Medium Yes Manual .env file (600) Medium Low Yes Manual 1Password / Bitwarden High Medium Yes Manual Short-lived tokens Highest Medium Yes Automatic Plaintext in mcp.json None None Yes Manual

docs.title: Restrict ArgoCD RBAC
docs.text:
Instead of using the admin account, create a dedicated service account with minimal permissions:

# In argocd-cm ConfigMap
accounts.cursor-mcp: apiKey
accounts.cursor-mcp.enabled: "true"

# In argocd-rbac-cm ConfigMap
policy.csv: |
  p, role:mcp-readonly, applications, get, */*, allow
  p, role:mcp-readonly, applications, list, */*, allow
  p, role:mcp-readonly, clusters, list, *, allow
  g, cursor-mcp, role:mcp-readonly

docs.title: Set token expiry at generation time
docs.text: argocd account generate-token --account cursor-mcp --expires-in 720h

docs.title: Audit token usage
docs.text:
Check ArgoCD server logs for API calls made with the MCP token:

kubectl logs -n argocd deployment/argocd-server | grep "cursor-mcp"

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Never store long-lived ArgoCD tokens as plaintext in config files. Use a wrapper script to inject the token at runtime from a secure store — macOS Keychain for local dev, or a password manager CLI for cross-platform setups. For production-adjacent environments, prefer short-lived tokens with restricted RBAC.

docs.title: Ceph-Ansible to Cephadm Migration Lab
docs.text:
This document covers setting up a bare-minimum VM-based Ceph lab using ceph-ansible, followed by a migration plan to cephadm/cephadm-ansible. The goal is to simulate a real-world migration path in a resource-constrained lab environment.

Why Migrate?

ceph-ansible has been deprecated since Ceph Pacific. cephadm is the officially supported deployment and orchestration tool from Ceph Quincy onwards. Planning and testing the migration in a lab is critical before touching production clusters.

docs.title: Lab Topology & Bare Minimum Specs
docs.text:
A minimal 3-node Ceph cluster plus 1 admin/deploy node. All VMs can run on a single hypervisor (KVM/libvirt, VirtualBox, or Proxmox).

Role Hostname vCPU RAM OS Disk OSD Disk(s) IP (example) Admin/Deploy ceph-admin 2 2 GB 20 GB — 192.168.56.10 Mon + OSD ceph-node1 2 3 GB 20 GB 1 × 10 GB 192.168.56.11 Mon + OSD ceph-node2 2 3 GB 20 GB 1 × 10 GB 192.168.56.12 Mon + OSD ceph-node3 2 3 GB 20 GB 1 × 10 GB 192.168.56.13

Total Resources

~8 vCPUs, ~11 GB RAM, ~100 GB disk. This fits comfortably on a 16 GB laptop or a small cloud instance.

OSD Disks

Each OSD node needs a separate raw/unformatted virtual disk (not a partition on the OS disk). In libvirt/VirtualBox, add a second .qcow2 or .vdi disk to each node.

docs.title: Base OS Preparation (All Nodes)
docs.text:
Use Ubuntu 22.04 LTS (Jammy) or CentOS Stream 9. The examples below use Ubuntu. 

    # Set hostnames (run on each respective node)
    sudo hostnamectl set-hostname ceph-admin   # on admin
    sudo hostnamectl set-hostname ceph-node1   # on node1
    sudo hostnamectl set-hostname ceph-node2   # on node2
    sudo hostnamectl set-hostname ceph-node3   # on node3

Add entries to /etc/hosts on all nodes:

/etc/hosts 

    192.168.56.10  ceph-admin
    192.168.56.11  ceph-node1
    192.168.56.12  ceph-node2
    192.168.56.13  ceph-node3

    # Update and install prerequisites (all nodes)
    sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y
    sudo apt install -y python3 python3-pip python3-venv chrony lvm2

docs.title: SSH Key Setup (Admin Node)
docs.text:
# On ceph-admin
    ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -N "" -f ~/.ssh/id_ed25519

    # Copy to all nodes (including admin itself)
    for host in ceph-admin ceph-node1 ceph-node2 ceph-node3; do
        ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub ubuntu@${host}
    done

docs.title: NTP Sync (All Nodes)
docs.text:
Ceph is sensitive to clock skew. Ensure chrony is running: 

    sudo systemctl enable --now chrony
    chronyc tracking

docs.title: Install ceph-ansible (Admin Node)
docs.text:
Ceph Release

This lab uses Ceph Quincy (17.2.x) as the last release with ceph-ansible support. For Pacific (16.2.x), adjust the branch accordingly. 

    # On ceph-admin
    sudo apt install -y git ansible

    git clone https://github.com/ceph/ceph-ansible.git -b stable-7.0
    cd ceph-ansible

    pip3 install -r requirements.txt

docs.title: Ansible Inventory
docs.text:
ceph-ansible/inventory/hosts 

    [mons]
    ceph-node1
    ceph-node2
    ceph-node3

    [osds]
    ceph-node1
    ceph-node2
    ceph-node3

    [mgrs]
    ceph-node1

    [mdss]

    [rgws]

    [clients]
    ceph-admin

docs.title: Group Variables
docs.text:
ceph-ansible/group_vars/all.yml 

    ---
    ceph_origin: repository
    ceph_repository: community
    ceph_stable_release: quincy
    ceph_repository_type: cdn

    monitor_interface: enp0s8          # adjust to your VM network interface
    public_network: "192.168.56.0/24"
    cluster_network: "192.168.56.0/24" # same as public in lab

    dashboard_enabled: true
    dashboard_admin_user: admin
    dashboard_admin_password: admin123  # lab only — never use in production

    ceph_conf_overrides:
      global:
        osd_pool_default_size: 2       # 2 replicas for a 3-node lab
        osd_pool_default_min_size: 1
        mon_allow_pool_delete: true

ceph-ansible/group_vars/osds.yml 

    ---
    osd_scenario: lvm
    osd_objectstore: bluestore

    lvm_volumes:
      - data: /dev/vdb    # the second virtual disk on each OSD node

Finding the OSD Disk Device

Run lsblk on each OSD node to confirm the device name. It's typically /dev/vdb or /dev/sdb depending on your hypervisor.

docs.title: Ansible Config
docs.text:
ceph-ansible/ansible.cfg 

    [defaults]
    inventory = inventory/hosts
    remote_user = ubuntu
    host_key_checking = False
    retry_files_enabled = False
    log_path = ./ansible.log

    [privilege_escalation]
    become = True
    become_method = sudo
    become_user = root

docs.title: Deploy the Ceph Cluster
docs.text:
cd ~/ceph-ansible

    # Run the site playbook
    ansible-playbook site.yml -i inventory/hosts

Deployment Time

First run takes ~15-25 minutes depending on download speeds. Subsequent runs are faster due to caching.

docs.title: Validate the Cluster
docs.text:
SSH into any mon node and check: 

    sudo ceph -s
    sudo ceph osd tree
    sudo ceph health detail
    sudo ceph df

Expected Healthy Output 

      cluster:
        id:     a1b2c3d4-e5f6-7890-abcd-ef1234567890
        health: HEALTH_OK

      services:
        mon: 3 daemons, quorum ceph-node1,ceph-node2,ceph-node3
        mgr: ceph-node1(active)
        osd: 3 osds: 3 up, 3 in

      data:
        pools:   1 pools, 1 pgs
        objects: 0 objects, 0 B
        usage:   3.0 GiB used, 27 GiB / 30 GiB avail
        pgs:     1 active+clean

Create a test pool to confirm writes work: 

    sudo ceph osd pool create testpool 32
    sudo rados -p testpool bench 10 write --no-cleanup
    sudo rados -p testpool bench 10 seq

docs.title: Migration Overview
docs.text:
The migration follows the official Ceph documentation pattern: 

    graph LR
        A[ceph-ansible cluster] --> B[Install cephadm on a mon]
        B --> C[Adopt existing daemons]
        C --> D[cephadm manages all daemons]
        D --> E[Remove ceph-ansible artifacts]

Key Constraints

  • Migration must be done one daemon type at a time (mons first, then mgrs, then OSDs).
  • The cluster remains operational throughout — no downtime required.
  • Always back up /etc/ceph/ and monitor keyrings before starting.

docs.title: Pre-Migration Checklist
docs.text:
• Cluster is HEALTH_OK (or only known warnings)
  • All OSDs are up and in
  • No recovery/backfill in progress
  • /etc/ceph/ceph.conf and all keyrings are backed up
  • NTP is synced on all nodes
  • Docker or Podman is installed on all nodes
  • Ceph version is at least Quincy 17.2.x
    # Verify cluster health
    sudo ceph -s
    sudo ceph osd tree

    # Backup critical configs
    sudo tar czf /root/ceph-backup-pre-migration.tar.gz \
        /etc/ceph/ \
        /var/lib/ceph/bootstrap-osd/ \
        /var/lib/ceph/bootstrap-mds/ \
        /var/lib/ceph/bootstrap-rgw/

docs.title: Install Container Runtime (All Nodes)
docs.text:
cephadm runs Ceph daemons in containers. Install Podman (preferred) or Docker: 

    # On all ceph nodes
    sudo apt install -y podman
    podman --version

docs.title: Install cephadm (Mon Node — ceph-node1)
docs.text:
# On ceph-node1 (a mon node)
    sudo apt install -y cephadm

    # Verify
    cephadm version

Match Versions

Ensure the cephadm version matches your running Ceph cluster version. For Quincy: 

    sudo cephadm install --release quincy

docs.title: Prepare cephadm to Adopt the Cluster
docs.text:
# On ceph-node1
    # Tell cephadm about the existing cluster
    sudo cephadm adopt --style legacy --name mon.ceph-node1

    # Verify the mon is now running in a container
    sudo cephadm ls

Expected Output from cephadm ls 

    [
        {
            "style": "cephadm:v1",
            "name": "mon.ceph-node1",
            "fsid": "a1b2c3d4-e5f6-7890-abcd-ef1234567890",
            "systemd_unit": "ceph-a1b2c3d4-mon@ceph-node1",
            "enabled": true,
            "state": "running"
        }
    ]

docs.title: Step 1 — Adopt Monitors
docs.text:
Adopt monitors one at a time. Verify quorum after each adoption. 

    # On ceph-node1 (already adopted above)
    # Now adopt remaining mons — run cephadm on each respective node

    # On ceph-node2
    sudo cephadm adopt --style legacy --name mon.ceph-node2

    # On ceph-node3
    sudo cephadm adopt --style legacy --name mon.ceph-node3

    # Verify quorum
    sudo ceph mon stat
    sudo ceph -s

docs.title: Step 2 — Adopt Manager
docs.text:
# On ceph-node1 (where mgr runs)
    sudo cephadm adopt --style legacy --name mgr.ceph-node1

docs.title: Step 3 — Adopt OSDs
docs.text:
Adopt each OSD individually. Check OSD status after each adoption. 

    # Find OSD IDs on each node
    sudo ceph osd tree

    # On ceph-node1
    sudo cephadm adopt --style legacy --name osd.0

    # On ceph-node2
    sudo cephadm adopt --style legacy --name osd.1

    # On ceph-node3
    sudo cephadm adopt --style legacy --name osd.2

    # Verify all OSDs are up
    sudo ceph osd tree

OSD Adoption

OSD adoption is the most sensitive step. If an OSD fails to start after adoption, check logs with: 

    sudo cephadm logs --name osd.<id>
    journalctl -u ceph-<fsid>@osd.<id>.service

docs.title: Using cephadm-ansible for Remaining Operations
docs.text:
Once all daemons are adopted, use cephadm-ansible for orchestrated management. 

    # On ceph-admin
    git clone https://github.com/ceph/cephadm-ansible.git
    cd cephadm-ansible

docs.title: cephadm-ansible Inventory
docs.text:
cephadm-ansible/inventory/hosts 

    [admin]
    ceph-node1

    [clients]
    ceph-admin

Note

cephadm-ansible only needs to know the admin node (where cephadm shell runs). cephadm itself manages the cluster topology via its orchestrator.

docs.title: Preflight Playbook
docs.text:
ansible-playbook -i inventory/hosts cephadm-preflight.yml \
        -e "ceph_origin=repository" \
        -e "ceph_repository=community" \
        -e "ceph_stable_release=quincy"

docs.title: Post-Migration Cleanup
docs.text:
After all daemons are adopted and running in containers: 

    # Disable and remove legacy ceph packages (on all nodes)
    sudo systemctl disable ceph.target
    sudo apt remove -y ceph-mon ceph-osd ceph-mgr ceph-mds ceph-common || true

    # Verify everything runs via cephadm
    sudo cephadm ls
    sudo ceph orch ps
    sudo ceph orch ls

docs.title: Final Validation
docs.text:
# Full cluster health
    sudo ceph -s
    sudo ceph health detail

    # All daemons managed by cephadm
    sudo ceph orch ps

    # Test I/O on existing pool
    sudo rados -p testpool bench 10 write --no-cleanup
    sudo rados -p testpool bench 10 seq

    # Dashboard should still be accessible
    sudo ceph mgr services

Expected Final State 

      cluster:
        id:     a1b2c3d4-e5f6-7890-abcd-ef1234567890
        health: HEALTH_OK

      services:
        mon: 3 daemons, quorum ceph-node1,ceph-node2,ceph-node3
        mgr: ceph-node1(active)
        osd: 3 osds: 3 up, 3 in

      data:
        pools:   2 pools, 33 pgs
        objects: 42 objects, 1.2 MiB
        usage:   3.1 GiB used, 26.9 GiB / 30 GiB avail
        pgs:     33 active+clean

docs.title: Tips & Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Issue Resolution cephadm adopt fails with permission error Ensure passwordless sudo is configured for the user OSD won't start after adoption Check LVM is intact: sudo lvs, sudo vgs Mon quorum lost during adoption Adopt only one mon at a time, verify quorum between each Container image pull fails Pre-pull on all nodes: sudo podman pull quay.io/ceph/ceph:v17 Clock skew warnings Verify chrony: chronyc tracking on all nodes Dashboard inaccessible after migration Re-enable: sudo ceph mgr module enable dashboard

References

  • Ceph cephadm adoption docs
  • ceph-ansible GitHub
  • cephadm-ansible GitHub
  • Ceph Quincy release notes

docs.title: How kubeconfig Is Generated by Kubespray and k3d
docs.text: kubeconfig files tell kubectl (and other clients) how to reach a cluster and how to authenticate. By default, kubectl looks for a file named config in ~/.kube/, but tools like Kubesprayandk3d generate and manage additional kubeconfigs for the clusters they create.123

docs.title: Common kubeconfig concepts
docs.text:
A kubeconfig file is a YAML document containing:

  • clusters — API server endpoints and TLS settings.
  • users — credentials (client certificates, tokens, etc.).
  • contexts — a tuple of (cluster, user, namespace) to make a "profile".

kubectl chooses which cluster to talk to based on the current context. You can point it to a specific file by:

  • Setting KUBECONFIG=/path/to/kubeconfig, or
  • Using kubectl --kubeconfig=/path/to/kubeconfig ...4251

Tip

You can merge multiple kubeconfig files by setting KUBECONFIG to a colon-separated list of paths, e.g. export KUBECONFIG=~/.kube/config:~/kubeconfigs/admin.conf

docs.title: Kubespray: kubeconfig generation flow
docs.text: Kubespray is an Ansible playbook collection that installs a production-grade Kubernetes cluster on your own hosts. As part of the control-plane bootstrap, it generates kubeconfig files on the master/control-plane nodes and optionally on worker nodes.678

docs.title: Where kubeconfig lives with Kubespray
docs.text:
On each control-plane node, Kubespray (via kubeadm) creates:

File Purpose /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf Admin kubeconfig (cluster-admin privileges) /etc/kubernetes/kubelet.conf Kubelet client config /etc/kubernetes/controller-manager.conf Controller manager config /etc/kubernetes/scheduler.conf Scheduler config

Localhost-bound by default

Kubespray kubeconfigs generally point to localhost on control-plane nodes, or to a local nginx proxy / external load balancer if configured.86

"The kubeconfig files generated will point to localhost (on kube_control_planes) and kube_node hosts will connect either to a localhost nginx proxy or to a loadbalancer if configured."6

Practically:

  • Control-plane nodes talk to the API server via https://127.0.0.1:6443.
  • Worker nodes may point at a local nginx proxy or a dedicated external load balancer.86

docs.title: How Kubespray generates kubeconfig
docs.text:
1. kubeadm init on the first control-plane node

kubeadm generates a CA and server/client certificates, then writes admin.conf and other component configs under /etc/kubernetes/.98

  1. Ansible templates and copies kubeconfig

Kubespray's Ansible roles read admin.conf and adjust the server: field to point to either https://127.0.0.1:6443 or an HA load balancer.68

  1. Expose kubeconfig to the operator machine (manual step)

Copy the file from the control-plane node to your workstation: [code] scp ubuntu@cp-1:/etc/kubernetes/admin.conf ~/kubeconfigs/admin.conf export KUBECONFIG=~/kubeconfigs/admin.conf kubectl get nodes

[/code]

Or merge it into ~/.kube/config using kubectl config commands.24

  1. Using kubeconfig on the control-plane node directly

SSH to a control-plane node and run: [code] export KUBECONFIG=/etc/kubernetes/admin.conf kubectl get nodes

[/code]

This talks to the API server bound to 127.0.0.1:6443 on that host.86

docs.title: Key characteristics of Kubespray kubeconfig
docs.text:
• Source of truth is admin.conf produced by kubeadm on the first control-plane node.98
  • Transport is https with client certs (cluster-admin credentials).
  • Endpoints are typically localhost or a configured load balancer.68
  • Distribution to operators is a manual step — Kubespray does not write kubeconfig on your laptop.

docs.title: k3d: kubeconfig generation flow
docs.text: k3d runs k3s (a lightweight Kubernetes distribution) inside Docker containers. Unlike Kubespray, it has direct control over both the control-plane and the CLI environment, so it can generate and update kubeconfigs on the fly.1011

docs.title: Where kubeconfig lives with k3d
docs.text:
By default, k3d integrates with your existing kubeconfig:

  • It detects the "default" kubeconfig as the file pointed to by KUBECONFIG (if it references exactly one file), or ~/.kube/config if KUBECONFIG is unset.1110

k3d can also:

  • Write a cluster-specific kubeconfig to ~/.k3d/kubeconfig-<cluster-name>.yaml.11
  • Merge cluster details into your default kubeconfig and optionally switch context.

docs.title: How k3d generates kubeconfig during cluster creation
docs.text:
When you run k3d cluster create mycluster, the steps are:

  1. k3s server inside Docker creates its own kubeconfig

k3s writes /etc/rancher/k3s/k3s.yaml inside the container, containing the API endpoint and certs.12

  1. k3d reads and adapts that kubeconfig

k3d inspects the container, reads the internal kubeconfig, and rewrites the server: URL to a host-accessible endpoint (e.g., https://0.0.0.0:<mapped-port>).11

  1. k3d writes or merges kubeconfig on the host

By default (k3d v5.x+), --kubeconfig-update-default is enabled:11

 * Merges the new cluster into `~/.kube/config` (or `$KUBECONFIG`).
 * Does **not** switch context unless you also pass `--kubeconfig-switch-context`.

[code] kubectl config get-contexts # shows k3d-mycluster

[/code]

docs.title: k3d kubeconfig commands
docs.text:
Write standalone Print to stdout Merge into file 

    k3d kubeconfig write mycluster
    # creates ~/.k3d/kubeconfig-mycluster.yaml

    k3d kubeconfig get mycluster > ./kubeconfig-mycluster.yaml
    export KUBECONFIG=./kubeconfig-mycluster.yaml
    kubectl get nodes

    k3d kubeconfig merge mycluster --output some/other/file.yaml
    # or into default kubeconfig:
    k3d kubeconfig merge mycluster --kubeconfig-merge-default

Switching context

Add --kubeconfig-switch-context to any merge/write command to make the new cluster the active context.1011

docs.title: Example flows with k3d
docs.text:
Default — merge into ~/.kube/config 

    k3d cluster create mycluster
    kubectl config get-contexts
    kubectl config use-context k3d-mycluster
    kubectl get nodes

k3d pulls the kubeconfig from k3s inside Docker, merges it into your default kubeconfig, and leaves the current context unchanged unless --kubeconfig-switch-context is used.11

Standalone kubeconfig only 

    k3d cluster create mycluster --kubeconfig-update-default=false
    k3d kubeconfig write mycluster
    export KUBECONFIG=~/.k3d/kubeconfig-mycluster.yaml
    kubectl get nodes

Useful for isolating cluster configs in scripts or demos.1011

docs.title: Key characteristics of k3d kubeconfig
docs.text:
• Automatic — k3d always has a kubeconfig per cluster; merge or write standalone.11
  • Context management — optionally switch context via --kubeconfig-switch-context.1011
  • Host-visible endpoint — rewrites the server: URL from the k3s internal address to a host-reachable address/port.

docs.title: Summary: Kubespray vs k3d
docs.text:
Aspect Kubespray k3d Primary environment Bare-metal/VM hosts k3s inside Docker (local/dev) Where kubeconfig is created /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf via kubeadm Inside k3s container, exported to host Default endpoint https://127.0.0.1:6443 or nginx/LB Host-reachable mapped Docker port How operator gets kubeconfig :material-hand-right: Manual copy from node Auto-merged into default kubeconfig Integration with ~/.kube/config Not automatic Automatic (unless disabled) Context switching Manual via kubectl config use-context Optional via --kubeconfig-switch-context

Both tools produce standard kubeconfig files — the main differences are wherethey originate andhow much automation they provide for placing and merging them.611

docs.title: KServe vs vLLM vs Kubeflow — Understanding the ML Serving Stack
docs.text: If you're deploying machine learning models on Kubernetes, you've probably encountered KServe, vLLM, and Kubeflow. They sound like they do similar things, but they operate at completely different layers of the stack — and are often used together, not as alternatives.

docs.title: The three layers at a glance
docs.text:
graph TB
    subgraph Platform["Kubeflow (ML Platform)"]
        NB[Notebooks]
        PL[Pipelines]
        TR[Training Operator]
        KT[Katib - Tuning]
        subgraph Serving["KServe (Serving Layer)"]
            AS[Autoscaling]
            TF[Traffic Splitting]
            subgraph Engine["vLLM (Inference Engine)"]
                PA[PagedAttention]
                CB[Continuous Batching]
                TP[Tensor Parallelism]
            end
        end
    end
Layer Tool One-liner Engine vLLM "Load weights, run inference, manage KV cache" Serving KServe "Scale pods, split traffic, route requests" Platform Kubeflow "Train, tune, version, deploy, monitor — the full lifecycle"

docs.title: vLLM — The inference engine
docs.text: vLLM is the thing that actually loads model weights into GPU memory, runs the forward pass, manages the KV cache, and generates tokens. It's the engine inside the car.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
• Loads LLM weights (Llama, Mistral, Qwen, DeepSeek, etc.)
  • Implements PagedAttention for efficient KV cache management
  • Continuous batching of concurrent requests
  • Tensor parallelism across multiple GPUs
  • Quantization support (AWQ, GPTQ, FP8, NVFP4)
  • Exposes an OpenAI-compatible API

docs.title: When to use vLLM alone
docs.text:
You're running a single model on a single machine or a manually managed deployment. You handle scaling and routing yourself (or don't need it).

vllm serve meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct \
  --dtype auto \
  --max-model-len 4096 \
  --gpu-memory-utilization 0.9

That gives you http://localhost:8000/v1/chat/completions — an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, ready to use.

Competitors

TGI (HuggingFace), SGLang, TensorRT-LLM, llama.cpp, Ollama

docs.title: KServe — The model serving platform
docs.text: KServe is a Kubernetes-native model serving framework. It handles the infrastructure concerns around deploying, scaling, and managing inference workloads. It's the fleet management system that decides how many cars to deploy and routes passengers to them.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
• Autoscaling — scale-to-zero, scale on GPU utilization or queue depth
  • Canary rollouts — traffic splitting between model versions
  • Request routing and load balancing
  • Multi-model serving on shared infrastructure
  • Standardized V2 Inference Protocol
  • Model storage abstraction (S3, GCS, PVC)
  • Transformer → Predictor → Explainer pipeline pattern

docs.title: KServe with vLLM as backend
docs.text:
apiVersion: serving.kserve.io/v1beta1
kind: InferenceService
metadata:
  name: llama-3
spec:
  predictor:
    model:
      modelFormat:
        name: vLLM
      runtime: kserve-vllm
      storageUri: s3://models/llama-3-8b
      resources:
        limits:
          nvidia.com/gpu: 1

KServe handles the scaling and traffic; vLLM handles the actual inference inside each pod.

Competitors

Seldon Core, Triton Inference Server, Ray Serve, BentoML

docs.title: Kubeflow — The full ML platform
docs.text: Kubeflow operates at the highest layer. It's the entire ML factory — from notebook experimentation to production serving. KServe is actually a component within Kubeflow.

docs.title: Components
docs.text: Component What it does Notebooks Managed Jupyter environments on K8s Pipelines (KFP) DAG-based ML workflow orchestration Katib Automated hyperparameter tuning Training Operator Distributed training (PyTorch, TensorFlow, MPI) KServe Model serving with autoscaling Model Registry Versioned model storage and metadata

docs.title: A typical Kubeflow LLM workflow
docs.text:
1. Notebooks      → Experiment with model architectures, test prompts
2. Pipelines      → Define: download base model → fine-tune → evaluate → register
3. Training Op    → Run distributed fine-tuning on multi-GPU nodes
4. Katib          → Sweep learning rates, LoRA ranks, batch sizes
5. Model Registry → Store the winning checkpoint with metadata
6. KServe         → Deploy with autoscaling and canary rollout
7. vLLM           → The runtime inside each pod doing actual inference

When to use Kubeflow

You have a team of ML engineers who need shared infrastructure for the full lifecycle — experimentation, training, tuning, versioning, AND serving.

docs.title: KServe vs vLLM
docs.text: Concern vLLM KServe Layer Inference engine Serving orchestrator Runs on Bare metal, Docker, K8s pod Kubernetes only Scaling Single instance (manual) Auto-scales pods up/down Model loading Local path or HuggingFace S3, GCS, PVC, model registry Traffic management None Canary, A/B, traffic split GPU scheduling Uses what it's given Multi-model packing, scale-to-zero API OpenAI-compatible V2 Inference Protocol + OpenAI Batching Continuous batching Delegates to runtime (vLLM) KV cache PagedAttention N/A (engine concern)

docs.title: KServe standalone vs Kubeflow
docs.text: Concern KServe standalone Kubeflow Model serving  Yes  Yes (includes KServe) Training jobs  No  Yes Pipelines/workflows  No  Yes Experiment tracking  No  Yes Notebooks  No  Yes Multi-tenancy  No  Yes Install complexity Low High (Istio, Dex, many CRDs)

docs.title: Decision guide
docs.text: Scenario What you need "I just want to run an LLM fast" vLLM alone "I need autoscaling and traffic management" KServe + vLLM "I need to train, tune, version, AND serve models on K8s" Kubeflow (includes KServe) "I'm serving non-LLM models (sklearn, XGBoost)" KServe with built-in runtimes "I have a team needing shared ML infra" Kubeflow

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• vLLM = "make the model go fast" — the inference engine that generates tokens
  • KServe = "manage model deployments at scale" — the Kubernetes serving layer
  • Kubeflow = "the entire ML factory" — from notebook to production

They're complementary, not competing. vLLM runs inside KServe pods. KServe is a component of Kubeflow. Pick the layer that matches your operational needs — you can always adopt the layers above as your requirements grow.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The swift_retention_policy.py script helps you automatically set object expiration and clean up empty Swift containers after all objects have expired and been deleted.

Note

This script has only been tested with Freezer backup containers created in Swift, but it should work with any Swift containers and objects.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Requirements

  • Python Swift client installed
  • OpenStack credentials sourced
  • Access to Swift storage verified
    # Install Python Swift client
    pip install python-swiftclient

    # Source OpenStack credentials of your Flex cluster
    source ~/openrc

    # Verify access
    swift list

Make the script executable: 

    chmod +x swift_retention_policy.py

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
The script provides a complete workflow for container cleanup:

  • Set X-Delete-At on all objects in containers
  • Monitor containers until empty
  • Automatically delete empty containers
  • Single command for complete cleanup
  • Progress tracking and timeout protection

docs.title: Basic Examples
docs.text:
Quick Cleanup (5 min)Multiple ContainersExpiration Only (No Cleanup)Custom Check IntervalDry Run 

    ./swift_retention_policy.py -c freezer-bkp-lvm -m 5 --cleanup

    ./swift_retention_policy.py -c freezer-daily -c freezer-weekly -H 1 --cleanup

    ./swift_retention_policy.py -c freezer-bkp-lvm -d 7

    ./swift_retention_policy.py -c freezer-bkp-lvm -m 5 --cleanup --check-interval 30

    ./swift_retention_policy.py -c freezer-bkp-lvm -m 5 --cleanup --dry-run

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Container Not Being Deleted

Problem: Container shows as empty but won't delete.

Solutions:

  1. Check for hidden objects: [code] swift list freezer-bkp-lvm --prefix ""

[/code]

  1. Manual deletion: [code] swift delete freezer-bkp-lvm

[/code]

Objects Not Expiring

Problem: Objects have X-Delete-At set but aren't being deleted.

Solution: Verify the swift-object-expirer daemon is running and healthy on the Swift cluster.

Script Times Out

Problem: Script reaches max-wait before the container is empty.

Solution: Increase the max wait time: 

    ./swift_retention_policy.py -c container -m 5 --cleanup --max-wait 7200

docs.title: Deploy Freezer
docs.text:
Freezer is a disaster recovery and backup-as-a-service component for OpenStack. It provides a way to back up various resources, such as virtual machine instances, databases, and file systems.

It allows users to schedule backups, restore data, and manage the lifecycle of their backups to ensure data protection and business continuity within an OpenStack cloud.

This document outlines the deployment of OpenStack Freezer-Api, Freezer-Agent and Freezer-Scheduler using Genestack.

Freezer Architecture

Unlike typical OpenStack services, only the freezer-api resides and runs in the OpenStack cluster. The freezer-agent and freezer-scheduler run outside the cluster. The user can deploy freezer-agent and scheduler on VM/Baremetal etc. making it act as a dedicated Freezer-Client.

docs.title: Installing Freezer-Agent and Freezer-Scheduler on Freezer-Client
docs.text:
In this case it's assumed that your Freezer-Client is actually a VM which can talk to the openstack api endpoints of your flex cluster.

Note

In this case it's assumed Ubuntu OS is the OS of choice on the freezer-client VM. However, it can really be any OS as long as its able to run python, since all freezer-agent code runs inside the virtual environment.

Automated (Recommended)Manual

The install_freezer_client.sh script automates the entire Freezer client setup including package installation, virtual environment creation, configuration file generation, and client registration.

Script Location

scripts/freezer/install_freezer_client.sh in the Genestack repository.

The script will prompt you for the following inputs:

Input Description Example Keystone FQDN Public FQDN of your Keystone endpoint (without https:// or /v3) keystone.cloud.dev Freezer service password Password for the freezer user in keystone_authtoken (from Kubernetes secretfreezer-keystone-service-password) Client ID Unique identifier for this Freezer client backup-client-vm

Retrieving the Freezer service password

From your Genestack control plane node: 

    kubectl -n openstack get secret freezer-keystone-service-password \
      -o jsonpath='{.data.password}' | base64 -d; echo

Run the installer: 

    chmod +x scripts/freezer/install_freezer_client.sh
    ./scripts/freezer/install_freezer_client.sh

The script automatically:

  • Detects the OS, version, and architecture
  • Installs python3-dev and python3-venv (supports apt, dnf, yum)
  • Creates a Python virtual environment at ~/freezer-venv
  • Installs freezer and pymysql via pip
  • Generates ~/openrc with your Keystone credentials
  • Generates /etc/freezer/freezer-scheduler.conf
  • Generates ~/client_register_config.json with detected OS metadata
  • Validates DNS resolution for the Keystone endpoint (with troubleshooting hints on failure)
  • Checks HTTPS connectivity to the Keystone API
  • Registers the client with the Freezer API
  • Starts the freezer-scheduler automatically

DNS Resolution

The script validates DNS resolution before registering the client. If resolution fails, it will exit with actionable hints including /etc/hosts entries, nameserver configuration, and VPN connectivity checks.

To reactivate the environment in a new shell session: 

    source ~/freezer-venv/bin/activate
    source ~/openrc

Install packages and create a virtual environment: 

    sudo apt-get install python3-dev
    sudo apt install python3.12-venv
    sudo python3 -m venv freezer-venv
    source freezer-venv/bin/activate

    pip install pymysql
    pip install freezer

Now freezer binaries are available inside the virtual environment.

Create RC file with flex openstack cluster credentials like below example

openrc 

    # ==================== BASIC AUTHENTICATION ====================
    export OS_AUTH_URL="https://keystone.cloud.dev/v3"
    export OS_USERNAME=admin
    export OS_PASSWORD=password
    export OS_PROJECT_NAME=admin
    export OS_PROJECT_DOMAIN_NAME=default

docs.title: MongoDB backup to Swift
docs.text:
In this case, mongoDB's LVM (where mongoDB LVM volume is mounted) is backed up.

MongoDB operations

Make sure you quiesce any DB operations by stopping the mongodb service momentarily and then restarting it once the backup is completed.

Running Freezer commands

Freezer commands can only be run from inside the virtual environment. 

    sudo systemctl stop mongod
    sudo systemctl status mongod

    freezer-agent \
            --action backup \
            --lvm-srcvol /dev/mongo/mongo-1 \
            --lvm-volgroup mongo \
            --lvm-snapsize 2G \
            --lvm-snap-perm ro \
            --lvm-dirmount /tmp/lvm-snapshot-backup  \
            --path-to-backup /tmp/lvm-snapshot-backup \
            --storage swift \
            --container mongo-bkp-lvm \
            --backup-name mongo-bkp-lvm \
            --log-file mongo-bkp-lvm.log

    sudo systemctl start mongod
    sudo systemctl status mongod

docs.title: MongoDB restore from Swift
docs.text:
Restore operation involves quiescing mongoDB operations by stopping the mongodb service momentarily and then restarting it once the backup is completed. 

    sudo systemctl stop mongod
    sudo systemctl status mongod

    mkdir -p /tmp/mongodb-restore

    # Restore timestamp can be fetched by querying the swift objects in the backup container like below.
    # Swift authenticates using the S3 credentials available on Freezer-client VM.

    swift list --lh freezer-bkp-mongo-lvm

    # Note the timestamp of the first object in the container.

    freezer-agent \
            --action restore \
            --mode mongo \
            --restore-from-date "2026-01-20T07:43:59" \
            --restore-abs-path /tmp/mongodb-restore  \
            --storage swift \
            --container freezer-bkp-mongo-lvm \
            --backup-name freezer-bkp-mongo-lvm \
            --encrypt-pass-file /home/ubuntu/mongo-test/encryption-key.txt \
            --log-file freezer-bkp-mongo-lvm-rstr.log

    sudo rsync -a /tmp/mongodb-restore/ /var/lib/mongodb/
    sudo chown -R mongodb:mongodb /var/lib/mongodb

    sudo systemctl start mongod
    sudo systemctl status mongod

docs.title: Creating Sessions
docs.text:
A session acts as a high-level container that groups related backup and restore actions. It provides a unique identifier and metadata that applies to all jobs executed within it.

When you create a job, you typically want that job's executions to be tied to a specific session. This makes management easier, especially during recovery, as you can see all backup runs related to a single project or time period under one session ID.

  1. Create a session config file on the Freezer Client.

Sample session_file.json

session_file.json [code]{ "description": "Local Storage VM Backup Session", "name": "local_vm_backup", "freezer_session_version": 2, "jobs": [ "local_storage_vm_job" ], "schedule": { "schedule_date": "2025-10-07T13:31:00Z" } }

[/code]

  1. Register the session:

CommandExpected Output [code] freezer session-create --file session_file.json 

     freezer session-list

[/code] [code] Session c6a7fcfd06134b788f0a34e8454174b1 created

     +----------------------------------+---------------------------------+--------+--------+--------+
     | Session ID                       | Description                     | Status | Result | # Jobs |
     +----------------------------------+---------------------------------+--------+--------+--------+
     | c6a7fcfd06134b788f0a34e8454174b1 | Local Storage VM Backup Session | active | None   |      0 |
     +----------------------------------+---------------------------------+--------+--------+--------+

[/code]

  1. Note the session-id from above. Add an existing job to this session (job-id's are arbitrary): [code] freezer session-add-job \ --session-id c6a7fcfd06134b788f0a34e8454174b1 \ --job-id 9999

[/code]

  1. Start a session with a specific job (job-* are arbitrary):

CommandExpected Output [code] freezer session-start \ --session-id c6a7fcfd06134b788f0a34e8454174b1 \ --job-id 9999 \ --job-tag 0

[/code] [code] Session c6a7fcfd06134b788f0a34e8454174b1 start requested

[/code]

docs.title: Backup Retention Policy
docs.text:
Freezer backups stored in Swift can accumulate over time. The swift_retention_policy.py script automates object expiration and container cleanup for Freezer backup containers.

Location

The script is located at scripts/freezer_retention/swift_retention_policy.py in the Genestack repository.

Note

This script has only been tested with Freezer backup containers created in Swift, but should work with any S3 compatible containers and objects.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
pip install python-swiftclient
    source ~/openrc
    swift list

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
chmod +x scripts/freezer_retention/swift_retention_policy.py

Set expiration and auto-cleanupMultiple containersSet expiration only (no cleanup)Dry run 

    ./swift_retention_policy.py -c freezer-bkp-lvm -m 5 --cleanup

    ./swift_retention_policy.py -c freezer-daily -c freezer-weekly -H 1 --cleanup

    ./swift_retention_policy.py -c freezer-bkp-lvm -d 7

    ./swift_retention_policy.py -c freezer-bkp-lvm -m 5 --cleanup --dry-run

All available options 

    Time Options:
      -s, --seconds N           Delete after N seconds
      -m, --minutes N           Delete after N minutes
      -H, --hours N             Delete after N hours
      -d, --days N              Delete after N days
      -M, --months N            Delete after N months
      -t, --delete-at UNIX      Delete at specific timestamp

    Cleanup Options:
      --cleanup                 Monitor and delete containers when empty
      --check-interval SECONDS  Seconds between checks (default: 60)
      --max-wait SECONDS        Maximum time to wait (default: 3600)

    Other Options:
      --dry-run                 Show what would be done
      -v, --verbose             Verbose output

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
The script operates in two phases:

  1. Sets X-Delete-At headers on all objects in the specified containers
  2. Monitors containers and automatically deletes them once empty (when --cleanup is used)
Container Status Description Auto-Delete? empty No objects remaining Yes not_found Container does not exist N/A has_permanent_objects Objects without X-Delete-At No waiting_for_expiration Objects not yet past expiry No waiting_for_expirer Expired but not yet removed by Swift No

Recommended check intervals

Expiration Window Check Interval < 10 minutes 30-60 seconds 1-24 hours 5-15 minutes > 1 day 30-60 minutes 
    # Short expiration
    ./swift_retention_policy.py -c container -m 5 --cleanup --check-interval 30

    # Long expiration
    ./swift_retention_policy.py -c container -d 1 --cleanup --check-interval 1800

Set a max wait time

Prevent the script from running indefinitely: 

    ./swift_retention_policy.py -c container -m 5 --cleanup --max-wait 3600

For full documentation and troubleshooting, see Freezer Backup Retention Policy.

docs.title: Magnum Enablement
docs.text:
OpenStack Magnum is the container orchestration service within the OpenStack ecosystem, designed to provide an easy-to-use interface for deploying and managing container clusters, such as Kubernetes.

Magnum enables cloud users to harness the power of containerization by allowing them to create and manage container clusters as first-class resources within the OpenStack environment. This service integrates seamlessly with other OpenStack components, enabling containers to take full advantage of OpenStack’s networking, storage, and compute capabilities. In this document, we will outline the deployment of OpenStack Magnum using Genestack. By utilizing Genestack, the deployment of Magnum is streamlined, allowing organizations to efficiently manage and scale containerized applications alongside traditional virtual machine workloads within their cloud infrastructure.

Overview

This comprehensive guide covers the complete installation process from management cluster setup to workload cluster deployment using Kubespray,Cluster API (CAPI), andOpenStack Magnum.

Note

Before Magnum can be deployed, you must setup and deploy Barbican first.

docs.title: Management Cluster Installation
docs.text:
What is a Management Cluster?

The management cluster is a separate, dedicated Kubernetes clusterthat hosts Cluster API (CAPI) controllers. It manages the lifecycle of workload clusters, handling provisioning, scaling, and upgrades.

This isnotthe existing Genestack Kubernetes cluster. The management cluster must be provisioned as a standalone cluster on dedicated infrastructure, typically VMs created by theadmin account (not tenant accounts). These VMs serve as the CAPI control plane and should be treated as part of your cloud infrastructure, similar to how the Genestack controllers are managed.

In summary:

  • You need to create new VMs (3 nodes recommended for HA) to host this cluster.
  • These VMs should be provisioned by the admin , not in tenant/user accounts.
  • The management cluster runs independently from the Genestack cluster and is responsible solely for managing CAPI-based workload clusters created through Magnum.
  • The Genestack cluster continues to run OpenStack services (Magnum API, conductor, etc.), while the management cluster runs the CAPI controllers that provision tenant workload clusters on OpenStack.

More Info on concepts can be found at cluster-api site.

docs.title: Create Management Cluster VM's
docs.text:
The management cluster infrastructure (project, network, instances, load balancer, etc.) can be provisioned automatically using the capi_cluster Ansible role included in Genestack, or manually if you prefer full control.

Automated (Recommended)Manual

The capi_cluster Ansible role automates the entire infrastructure setup including:

  • OpenStack project and user creation (in the service domain)
  • Network, subnet, router, and security group provisioning
  • Flavor, image (Ubuntu 24.04), keypair, and volume creation
  • Octavia load balancer for the Kubernetes API
  • Boot-from-volume instance provisioning (3 nodes)
  • Kubespray-based Kubernetes cluster installation
  • CAPI component initialization and etcd backup configuration

Prerequisites for the Ansible Role

  • Cinder volume service must be enabled (role uses boot-from-volume instances)
  • A pre-created shared external Neutron network (flat or VLAN)
  • Keystone admin credentials
  • Octavia service enabled (role creates a load balancer)
  • DNS server reachable from the external network that can resolve OpenStack service endpoints
  • OpenStack SDK installed on the Ansible control node (the Genestack venv is sufficient)
  • Sufficient Glance storage for the Ubuntu 24.04 image upload
  • If OpenStack endpoints are behind a TLS gateway, certificates must be signed by a well-known CA (self-signed certs will cause failures)

    ansible-playbook capi-mgmt-cluster-main.yaml \
      -e os_admin_password=<keystone_admin_password> \
      -e os_user_password=<capi_mgmt_user_password> \
      -e ext_net_id='<external_network_uuid>'

Refer to ansible/roles/capi_cluster/defaults/main.yml for the full list of variables.

The playbook will:

  1. Create the capi-mgmt-cluster-project in the service domain with appropriate quotas

docs.title: Kubespray: kubeconfig generation flow
docs.text: Kubespray is an Ansible playbook collection that installs a production-grade Kubernetes cluster on your own hosts. As part of the management cluster creation and hence control-plane bootstrap process, it generates kubeconfig files on the master/control-plane nodes and optionally on worker nodes.

docs.title: Where kubeconfig lives within Kubespray
docs.text:
On each control-plane node, Kubespray (via kubeadm) creates:

File Purpose /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf Admin kubeconfig (cluster-admin privileges) /etc/kubernetes/kubelet.conf Kubelet client config /etc/kubernetes/controller-manager.conf Controller manager config /etc/kubernetes/scheduler.conf Scheduler config

Localhost-bound by default

Kubespray kubeconfigs generally point to localhost on control-plane nodes, or to a local nginx proxy / external load balancer if configured.

"The kubeconfig files generated will point to localhost (on kube_control_planes) and kube_node hosts will connect either to a localhost nginx proxy or to a loadbalancer if configured."

Practically:

  • Control-plane nodes talk to the API server via https://127.0.0.1:6443.
  • Worker nodes may point at a local nginx proxy or a dedicated external load balancer.

docs.title: How Kubespray generates kubeconfig
docs.text:
1. kubeadm init on the first control-plane node

kubeadm generates a CA and server/client certificates, then writes admin.conf and other component configs under /etc/kubernetes/.

  1. Ansible templates and copies kubeconfig

Kubespray's Ansible roles read admin.conf and adjust the server: field to point to either https://127.0.0.1:6443 or an HA load balancer.

  1. Expose kubeconfig to the operator machine (manual step)

Copy the file from the control-plane node to your workstation: [code] scp ubuntu@cp-1:/etc/kubernetes/admin.conf ~/kubeconfigs/admin.conf export KUBECONFIG=~/kubeconfigs/admin.conf kubectl get nodes

[/code]

Or merge it into ~/.kube/config using kubectl config commands.

  1. Using kubeconfig on the control-plane node directly

SSH to a control-plane node and run: [code] export KUBECONFIG=/etc/kubernetes/admin.conf kubectl get nodes

[/code]

This talks to the API server bound to 127.0.0.1:6443 on that host.

docs.title: Key characteristics of Kubespray kubeconfig
docs.text:
• Source of truth is admin.conf produced by kubeadm on the first control-plane node.
  • Transport is https with client certs (cluster-admin credentials).
  • Endpoints are typically localhost or a configured load balancer.
  • Distribution to operators is a manual step — Kubespray does not write kubeconfig on your laptop.

Example: Precreated kubeconfig file 

    ---
    apiVersion: v1
    clusters:
    - cluster:
        certificate-authority-data: <cert-authority-data>
        server: https://192.168.1.254:6443
    name: cluster.local
    contexts:
    - context:
        cluster: cluster.local
        user: kubernetes-admin
    name: kubernetes-admin@cluster.local
    current-context: kubernetes-admin@cluster.local
    kind: Config
    preferences: {}
    users:
    - name: kubernetes-admin
    user:
        client-certificate-data: <client-cert-data>
        client-key-data: <client-key-data>

docs.title: Inject Management Cluster Kubeconfig into Magnum
docs.text:
Critical Step

This step is required before deploying or upgrading Magnum with CAPI support. Without it, the Magnum conductor cannot communicate with the CAPI controllers on the management cluster, and workload cluster provisioning will fail.

The Magnum CAPI Helm driver needs a kubeconfig file mounted inside the Magnum conductor pods so it can talk to the management cluster's Kubernetes API. The openstack-helm Magnum chart handles the secret creation and volume mount automatically — you just need to populate the CAPI overrides file with the management cluster credentials.

docs.title: Extract Credentials from Management Cluster Kubeconfig
docs.text:
From the management cluster master-01 (or wherever you have the kubeconfig), extract the three credential fields. These values are already base64-encoded inside the kubeconfig file. 

    # If using the kubeconfig generated by Kubespray
    export KUBECONFIG=/etc/kubernetes/admin.conf

    # Or if using the copied kubeconfig
    export KUBECONFIG=/var/tmp/capi_mgmt_cluster.kubeconfig

Extract ValuesOne-Liner Extraction 

    # Extract certificate-authority-data
    grep certificate-authority-data $KUBECONFIG | awk '{print $2}'

    # Extract client-certificate-data
    grep client-certificate-data $KUBECONFIG | awk '{print $2}'

    # Extract client-key-data
    grep client-key-data $KUBECONFIG | awk '{print $2}'

    # Extract server URL
    grep server $KUBECONFIG | awk '{print $2}'

    echo "=== API Server ==="
    kubectl config view --raw -o jsonpath='{.clusters[0].cluster.server}'
    echo ""

    echo "=== Certificate Authority Data ==="
    kubectl config view --raw -o jsonpath='{.clusters[0].cluster.certificate-authority-data}'
    echo ""

    echo "=== Client Certificate Data ==="
    kubectl config view --raw -o jsonpath='{.users[0].user.client-certificate-data}'
    echo ""

    echo "=== Client Key Data ==="
    kubectl config view --raw -o jsonpath='{.users[0].user.client-key-data}'
    echo ""

Keep These Values Handy

You will need all four values (API server URL, CA data, client cert, client key) for the next step. These are sensitive credentials — treat them like passwords.

docs.title: Populate the CAPI Helm Overrides File
docs.text:
From the genestack control-plane node, create or edit the CAPI overrides file that the install-magnum.sh script references: 

    vim /etc/genestack/helm-configs/magnum/magnum-helm-overrides-capi.yaml

/etc/genestack/helm-configs/magnum/magnum-helm-overrides-capi.yaml 

    conf:
      capi:
        enabled: true
        clusterName: capi-mgmt-cluster
        apiServer: https://192.168.1.254:6443
        certificateAuthorityData: <paste certificate-authority-data here>
        contextName: kubernetes-admin@cluster.local
        userName: kubernetes-admin
        clientCertificateData: <paste client-certificate-data here>
        clientKeyData: <paste client-key-data here>
      magnum:
        capi_helm:
          kubeconfig_file: /etc/magnum/kubeconfig.conf

Replace Placeholder Values

Field Source apiServer The management cluster load balancer VIP and port (e.g., https://192.168.1.254:6443) certificateAuthorityData The certificate-authority-data value from the kubeconfig contextName The context name from the kubeconfig (run kubectl config current-context) userName The user name from the kubeconfig (typically kubernetes-admin) clientCertificateData The client-certificate-data value from the kubeconfig clientKeyData The client-key-data value from the kubeconfig

How This Works Under the Hood

When the Magnum Helm chart (2025.1+) sees conf.capi.enabled: true, it:

  1. Assembles a standard kubeconfig YAML from the conf.capi fields (cluster name, API server, CA data, client cert, client key)
  2. Stores the assembled kubeconfig as a Kubernetes Secret in the openstack namespace
  3. Mounts that secret as a volume at /etc/magnum/kubeconfig.conf inside the Magnum conductor pods
  4. The conf.magnum.capi_helm.kubeconfig_file setting in magnum.conf tells the CAPI driver to read the kubeconfig from that mount path

This is why you don't need to manually create a secret or modify pod specs — the chart handles it all from the Helm values.

Optional: Point to Custom Helm Charts

If you maintain custom CAPI Helm charts for your environment, you can specify them: 

    conf:
      magnum:
        capi_helm:
          kubeconfig_file: /etc/magnum/kubeconfig.conf
          helm_chart_repo: https://rackerlabs.github.io/genestack-capi-helm-charts
          default_helm_chart_version: 0.1.0

docs.title: Upgrade Cluster
docs.text:
Before upgrading, verify that your cluster template supports the target Kubernetes version.

Check Current TemplateVerify Target Template ExistsPerform UpgradeMonitor Upgrade

Inspect the template currently associated with your cluster: 

    # Show the cluster's current template
    openstack coe cluster show k8s-flatcar -c cluster_template_id -f value

    # View template details including image and labels
    openstack coe cluster template show flatcar-template

Key fields to check:

Field What to Look For image_id Image must include the target Kubernetes version binaries labels.kube_tag If set, must match or support the target version coe Must be kubernetes

If upgrading to a new template, confirm it exists and has the correct configuration: 

    # List all available templates
    openstack coe cluster template list

    # Inspect the target template
    openstack coe cluster template show flatcar-template-v1-33

Ensure the target template's image contains the desired Kubernetes version. You can verify this by checking the image properties: 

    openstack image show <image_name_or_id> -c properties -f value

Look for kube_version or similar metadata confirming the bundled Kubernetes version.

Once you have confirmed template compatibility, run the upgrade: 

    openstack coe cluster upgrade k8s-flatcar \
      --cluster-template flatcar-template-v1-33

    # Watch cluster status during upgrade
    watch -n 10 'openstack coe cluster show k8s-flatcar -c status -c status_reason -f value'

Upgrade Considerations

  • The target template's image must contain the Kubernetes version you want to upgrade to.
  • Only single minor version jumps are recommended (e.g., v1.32 → v1.33). Skipping minor versions is unsupported.
  • Back up etcd and critical workloads before upgrading.
  • Nodes are upgraded in a rolling fashion; expect temporary capacity reduction during the process.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
Production Recommendations

High Availability: - Use 3 or 5 master nodes for control plane HA - Deploy across multiple availability zones if possible - Enable master load balancer

Security: - Disable Kubernetes Dashboard or secure it properly - Use network policies to restrict pod communication - Enable RBAC and pod security policies - Regularly update cluster and node images

Monitoring & Logging: - Deploy Prometheus and Grafana for monitoring - Set up centralized logging (ELK, Loki) - Enable cluster autoscaling for dynamic workloads

Backup & Recovery: - Regular etcd backups - Document cluster configuration - Test disaster recovery procedures

Resource Management: - Set resource requests and limits on pods - Use node affinity and taints/tolerations - Monitor cluster capacity and scale proactively

docs.title: What is Flatcar Container Linux?
docs.text:
About Flatcar

Flatcar Container Linux is a minimal, immutable Linux distribution designed for running containers. It's a fork of CoreOS Container Linux and provides:

  • Automatic updates with atomic rollback capability
  • Minimal attack surface with only essential packages
  • Container-optimized with Docker and containerd pre-installed
  • Kubernetes-ready with kubeadm, kubelet, and kubectl
  • Cloud-native with built-in cloud provider integrations

  • A KVM-capable host (physical or VM with nested virtualization)
  • Ubuntu 22.04 or similar Linux distribution

  • At least 20GB free disk space
  • 4GB+ RAM available
  • Internet connectivity for downloading dependencies

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Build Fails: Cannot Download Flatcar Image

Error: 

    ==> qemu.flatcar: Error downloading Flatcar image

Solutions:

  • Check internet connectivity
  • Verify firewall/proxy settings
  • Try a different Flatcar version
  • Manually download and specify image path

Build Fails: Ansible Provisioning Error

Error: 

    ==> qemu.flatcar: Provisioning with Ansible...
    ==> qemu.flatcar: fatal: [default]: FAILED!

Solutions:

  • Check Ansible version compatibility
  • Review build logs for specific errors
  • Verify Python dependencies are installed
  • Ensure sufficient disk space

Build Fails: QEMU/KVM Issues

Error: 

    ==> qemu.flatcar: Error launching VM

Solutions:

  • Verify KVM is enabled: lsmod | grep kvm
  • Check virtualization support: egrep -c '(vmx|svm)' /proc/cpuinfo
  • Ensure user has permissions: usermod -aG kvm,libvirt $USER
  • Restart libvirt: systemctl restart libvirtd

Image Upload Fails

Error: 

    Error: Unable to upload image to Glance

Solutions:

  • Verify OpenStack credentials
  • Check available storage quota
  • Ensure image file is not corrupted
  • Verify network connectivity to Glance API

    }

docs.title: MariaDB Operator Upgrade Runbook
docs.text:
Unified procedure for upgrading the MariaDB Operator Helm chart through the required progressive upgrade path. Sequential upgrades are mandatory due to CRD evolution and changes in replication and backup behaviour across versions.

Upgrade Path 

    0.36.0 → 0.37.1 → 0.38.1 → 25.8.4 → 25.10.4 → 26.3.0

Never Delete CRDs

Never delete CRDs during the upgrade — doing so will delete the MariaDB database pods. Uninstalling the operator Helm release alone does not cause DB downtime.

docs.title: Check current installed versions
docs.text:
helm list -A | grep mariadb
    helm status mariadb-operator -n mariadb-system
    helm status mariadb-operator-crds -n mariadb-system

docs.title: Update Helm repo and list available chart versions
docs.text:
helm repo update mariadb-operator
    helm search repo mariadb-operator/mariadb-operator --versions | head -20

docs.title: Pre-Upgrade Checks
docs.text:
Repeat Before Every Step

Run these checks before every upgrade step in the path.

docs.title: 1. Retrieve MariaDB root password
docs.text:
export MARIADB_ROOT_PASSWORD=$(kubectl get secret mariadb -n openstack \
      -o jsonpath='{.data.root-password}' | base64 -d)

docs.title: 2. Create full database backup
docs.text:
Identify the primary pod first, then run the backup from it: 

    PRIMARY_POD=$(kubectl get mariadb mariadb-cluster -n openstack -o jsonpath="{.status.currentPrimary}")
    echo "Primary pod: $PRIMARY_POD"

    kubectl exec -i "$PRIMARY_POD" -n openstack -- mariadb-dump \
      -u root -p"$MARIADB_ROOT_PASSWORD" \
      --all-databases \
      --single-transaction \
      --routines \
      --triggers > mariadb-cluster-full-backup-$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M).sql

Verify the backup: 

    ls -lh mariadb-cluster-full-backup-*.sql | tail -1

docs.title: 3. Check database sizes
docs.text:
kubectl exec -it "$PRIMARY_POD" -n openstack -- mariadb -u root -p"$MARIADB_ROOT_PASSWORD" -e "
    SELECT
      table_schema AS 'Database',
      ROUND(SUM(data_length + index_length) / 1024 / 1024, 2) AS 'Size_MB'
    FROM information_schema.tables
    WHERE table_schema NOT IN ('information_schema', 'performance_schema', 'mysql', 'sys')
    GROUP BY table_schema
    ORDER BY Size_MB DESC;"

docs.title: 4. Verify cluster health
docs.text:
Determine your cluster topology and run the appropriate checks:

Galera ClusterPrimary/Replica (Replication) 

    kubectl exec -it "$PRIMARY_POD" -n openstack -- mariadb -u root -p"$MARIADB_ROOT_PASSWORD" -e "
    SHOW STATUS LIKE 'wsrep_cluster_size';
    SHOW STATUS LIKE 'wsrep_cluster_status';
    SHOW STATUS LIKE 'wsrep_ready';"

Expected Values

Variable Expected wsrep_cluster_size 3 wsrep_cluster_status Primary wsrep_ready ON

Check the primary: 

    kubectl get mariadb mariadb-cluster -n openstack -o jsonpath="{.status.currentPrimary}"

Check replication status on each replica: 

    kubectl exec -it mariadb-cluster-1 -n openstack -- mariadb -u root -p"$MARIADB_ROOT_PASSWORD" -e "
    SHOW REPLICA STATUS\G"

Expected Values

Variable Expected Slave_IO_Running Yes Slave_SQL_Running Yes Seconds_Behind_Master 0

How to identify your topology

Check the MariaDB CR spec: 

    kubectl get mariadb mariadb-cluster -n openstack -o jsonpath="{.spec.galera.enabled}"

  • Returns true → Galera cluster
  • Returns empty/false → Primary/Replica (replication)

docs.title: 5. Verify cluster and pod status
docs.text:
kubectl get mariadb -n openstack
    kubectl get pods -l app.kubernetes.io/name=mariadb -n openstack
    kubectl get mariadb -n openstack -o yaml | grep -B1 autoFailover  #Read "Disclaimer" below
    kubectl get crd | grep mariadb

Disclaimer

Only present on versions >= 25.10.4

docs.title: 6. Verify current operator, webhook, and MariaDB image versions

Operator ImageWebhook ImageMariaDB Image 

    kubectl get pods -n mariadb-system -o wide

    kubectl get pods \
        $(kubectl get pods \
        -l app.kubernetes.io/name=mariadb-operator \
        -n mariadb-system \
        -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}') \
        -n mariadb-system \
        -o jsonpath="{..image}" | tr -s '[:space:]' '\n' | sort -u

    kubectl get pods \
        $(kubectl get pods \
        -l app.kubernetes.io/name=mariadb-operator-webhook \
        -n mariadb-system \
        -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}') \
        -n mariadb-system \
        -o jsonpath="{..image}" | tr -s '[:space:]' '\n' | sort -u

    kubectl get pods "$PRIMARY_POD" \
        -n openstack \
        -o jsonpath="{..image}" \
        | tr -s '[:space:]' '\n' | sort -u

docs.title: Per-Version Upgrade Procedure
docs.text: Repeat this procedure for each version in the upgrade path. Version-specific notes are listed in the next section.

docs.title: Preflight: Update MariaDB image and enable autoUpdateDataPlane
docs.text:
Update the MariaDB image in /opt/genestack/base-kustomize/mariadb-cluster/base/mariadb-replication.yaml to match the version compatible with the operator chart version being deployed. With every release update you must update this image beforeupgrading the mariadb-cluster (Galera or Replication).

Finding the compatible MariaDB image

Check the config.mariadbImage value in the upstream chart's values.yaml at the corresponding tag: 

    https://github.com/mariadb-operator/mariadb-operator/blob/v<VERSION>/deploy/charts/mariadb-operator/values.yaml

For example, for chart version25.8.4: 

    https://github.com/mariadb-operator/mariadb-operator/blob/v25.8.4/deploy/charts/mariadb-operator/values.yaml

shows mariadbImage: docker-registry1.mariadb.com/library/mariadb:11.8.2.

Update the image in the base manifest. Below is an example while upgrading to 25.8.4 compliant mariadb image:

mariadb-replication.yaml 

    spec:
      image: docker-registry1.mariadb.com/library/mariadb:11.8.2

Then set autoUpdateDataPlane: true using one of the following methods:

Kustomize Overlay (Recommended)Base Manifest

Edit /etc/genestack/kustomize/mariadb-cluster/overlay/kustomization.yaml:

kustomization.yaml 

    apiVersion: kustomize.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
    kind: Kustomization
    resources:
      - ../galera

    patches:
      - target:
          kind: MariaDB
          name: mariadb-cluster
          namespace: openstack
        patch: |-
          - op: replace
            path: /spec/updateStrategy/autoUpdateDataPlane
            value: true

Edit /etc/genestack/kustomize/mariadb-cluster/base/mariadb-replication.yaml:

mariadb-replication.yaml 

    spec:
      updateStrategy:
        autoUpdateDataPlane: true

Why autoUpdateDataPlane?

Enabling autoUpdateDataPlane uses aReplicasFirstPrimaryLaststrategy instead ofRollingUpdate. This applies to both cluster topologies:

  • Galera : Updates replica nodes first, then the primary. Avoids breaking the quorum by ensuring a majority of nodes remain available during the rollout.
  • Primary/Replica: Updates replicas first, then the primary. Prevents write downtime and data inconsistency by keeping the primary running until all replicas are updated and healthy.

In both cases, updating the primary first risks downtime and data inconsistency.

Apply the changes: 

    kubectl --namespace openstack apply -k /etc/genestack/kustomize/mariadb-cluster/overlay

docs.title: Step 1: Scale down operator and remove webhooks
docs.text:
kubectl scale deployment mariadb-operator -n mariadb-system --replicas=0
    kubectl scale deployment mariadb-operator-webhook -n mariadb-system --replicas=0
    kubectl delete validatingwebhookconfiguration mariadb-operator-webhook
    kubectl delete mutatingwebhookconfiguration mariadb-operator-webhook 2>/dev/null || true

docs.title: Step 2: Update chart version
docs.text:
Edit /etc/genestack/helm-chart-versions.yaml:

helm-chart-versions.yaml 

    mariadb-operator: <TARGET_VERSION>

Confirm the version has been set: 

    grep mariadb-operator /etc/genestack/helm-chart-versions.yaml

docs.title: Step 3: Uninstall and reinstall operator
docs.text:
helm uninstall mariadb-operator -n mariadb-system
    /opt/genestack/bin/install-mariadb-operator.sh

docs.title: Step 4: Verify deployment
docs.text:
helm list -A | grep mariadb
    kubectl get pods -n mariadb-system -o wide
    kubectl get pods <new-operator-pod> -n mariadb-system \
      -o jsonpath="{..image}" | tr -s '[:space:]' '\n' | sort -u

docs.title: Step 5: Post-upgrade validation
docs.text:
kubectl get pods -n openstack | grep mariadb
    kubectl get mariadb -n openstack

Run the cluster health checks from the pre-upgrade section again.

docs.title: Step 6: Disable autoUpdateDataPlane
docs.text:
Set autoUpdateDataPlane: false as per the preflight section and re-apply: 

    kubectl --namespace openstack apply -k /etc/genestack/kustomize/mariadb-cluster/overlay

docs.title: Step 7: Run the migration (Replication clusters only)
docs.text:
Replication Migration — Primary/Replica clusters only

This step is only required forPrimary/Replica (replication)clusters. If you are running aGalera cluster, skip this step.

After the operator upgrade, you must run the replication migration script to reset and re-establish replication on each replica pod.

The script automatically identifies the primary pod (skips it) and processes only the replicas. For each replica it:

  • Runs STOP SLAVE and RESET SLAVE ALL via kubectl exec
  • Deletes the pod so it gets recreated
  • Waits for it to come back ready
  • Verifies replication is working again

Set the required environment variables: 

    export MARIADB_NAME=mariadb-cluster
    export MARIADB_NAMESPACE=openstack
    export MARIADB_ROOT_PASSWORD=$(kubectl get secret mariadb -n openstack \
      -o jsonpath='{.data.root-password}' | base64 -d)

Save the script to a file (e.g. /tmp/migrate-replication.sh):

migrate-replication.sh (click to expand)

migrate-replication.sh 

    #!/bin/bash

    set -eo pipefail

    if [[ -z "$MARIADB_NAME" || -z "$MARIADB_NAMESPACE" || -z "$MARIADB_ROOT_PASSWORD" ]]; then
      echo "Error: MARIADB_NAME, MARIADB_NAMESPACE and MARIADB_ROOT_PASSWORD env vars must be set."
      exit 1
    fi

    function exec_sql {
      local pod=$1
      local sql=$2
      kubectl exec -n "$MARIADB_NAMESPACE" "$pod" -- mariadb -u root -p"$MARIADB_ROOT_PASSWORD" -e "$sql"
    }

    function wait_for_ready_replication {
      local pod=$1
      local timeout=300  # 5 minutes
      local interval=10  # Check every 10 seconds
      local elapsed=0

      echo "Waiting for ready replication on $pod..."

      while [[ $elapsed -lt $timeout ]]; do
          local status
          status=$(exec_sql "$pod" "SHOW REPLICA STATUS\G" | tee /tmp/replication_status_$pod_$MARIADB_NAMESPACE.txt)

          if grep -q "Slave_IO_Running: Yes" /tmp/replication_status_$pod_$MARIADB_NAMESPACE.txt && \
             grep -q "Slave_SQL_Running: Yes" /tmp/replication_status_$pod_$MARIADB_NAMESPACE.txt; then
            echo "Replication is ready on $pod."
            return 0
          fi

          echo "Replication not ready on $pod. Retrying in $interval seconds..."
          sleep $interval
          ((elapsed+=interval))
      done

      echo "Error: Replication did not become ready on $pod within 5 minutes."
      exit 1
    }

    echo "Migrating replication on $MARIADB_NAME instance..."

    PODS=$(kubectl get pods -n "$MARIADB_NAMESPACE" \
      -l app.kubernetes.io/instance=$MARIADB_NAME \
      -o jsonpath="{.items[*].metadata.name}")
    PRIMARY_POD=$(kubectl get mariadb "$MARIADB_NAME" -n "$MARIADB_NAMESPACE" \
      -o jsonpath="{.status.currentPrimary}")

    for POD in $PODS; do
      if [[ "$POD" == "$PRIMARY_POD" ]]; then
          printf "\nSkipping primary pod: $POD\n"
          continue
      fi
      printf "\nProcessing replica pod: $POD\n"

      echo "Resetting replication on $POD..."
      exec_sql "$POD" "STOP SLAVE 'mariadb-operator';"
      exec_sql "$POD" "RESET SLAVE 'mariadb-operator' ALL;"

      echo "Deleting pod $POD..."
      kubectl delete pod "$POD" -n "$MARIADB_NAMESPACE"

      echo "Waiting for pod $POD to become ready..."
      kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pod/"$POD" -n "$MARIADB_NAMESPACE" --timeout=5m
      echo "Pod $POD is ready."

      wait_for_ready_replication "$POD"
    done

    echo "Replication migration completed successfully on $MARIADB_NAME instance."

Make it executable and run: 

    chmod +x /tmp/migrate-replication.sh
    /tmp/migrate-replication.sh

Stuck replication threads

If stuck replication threads are observed, identify and kill them: 

    kubectl exec -it mariadb-cluster-1 -n openstack -- mariadb \
      -u root -p"$MARIADB_ROOT_PASSWORD" -e "SHOW PROCESSLIST;"
    kubectl exec -it mariadb-cluster-1 -n openstack -- mariadb \
      -u root -p"$MARIADB_ROOT_PASSWORD" -e "KILL <thread_id>;"

Skip 0.37.0

  • Release 0.37.1
  • Upgrade Guide 0.37.1

Follow the standard procedure above. No special steps required.

Skip 0.38.0

  • Release 0.38.1

Skip 25.08.0
